name: Fatima Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at an industrial bakery by the train yard, running the dough divider and the prover on the sliced-bread line. I start at ten at night, check the dough weights every twenty minutes, clear the divider when it clogs and watch the trays go into the prover, which is a warm cabinet where the dough rises. By six in the morning we've done about forty thousand loaves, and the lorries are waiting. I've done this for seven years, since my certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet of nights and the smell, honestly, even after seven years. What wears me out is sleeping in the day and the pay, which is the night rate but still lower than the dairy across town. My partner Jonas drives a delivery van, so our hours never match. Between us we keep the flat on Station Road, but there's under a month's money in the bank, usually less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it. I don't really talk about AI at work, and I'm not online much. If anyone asked, I'd say I never believed the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays as it is, which is what I want. I'm not interested in computers and I don't use the AI things. But my money doesn't get better either, so I'm still counting every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my nights, same as now. I'd try to pick up the extra Sunday shift before Christmas, when the bakery's busiest. I'd not change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the job, a bit worn about the money. Same as I've felt for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said usually less than a month saved. When does it get tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January, every year, after Christmas and with the heating bill. Every January the heating bill and the car insurance land in the same week, and my partner Jonas and I eat toast for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the bakery doing well, as far as you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As far as I know, yes, because everyone still buys bread. There was a rumour about a new owner last year, but nothing happened. People panic about rumours, and I try not to.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the fuss about AI.
I'd tell colleagues to just **get on** with the work.
think: I think my **job stays** as it is, which is what I want.
I think my **money** still doesn't get better, so I keep counting every week.
do: Carry on with **night shifts** at the bakery as normal.
Pick up the extra **Sunday shift** before Christmas.
Avoid changing anything else, including **new tools**.
feel: **Fine** about the job and **worn** about money, as for years.
S0.quote: Every January the heating bill and the car insurance land in the same week, and my partner Jonas and I eat toast for dinner.
fieldNote: Fatima's main pressure is a **January cash squeeze**, not technology.
She avoids AI and talks about it very **little**, at work or online.
She trusts bread demand and treats ownership rumours as **noise**.

steps.text: Keep working the night shift on the sliced-bread line
Take the extra Sunday shift before Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the offices that'll feel it, not people who make things. At work I'd keep my head down. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the bakery would look at the night shift, because nights cost more. If they could get a machine to watch the divider, they'd cut one of us. I'm not the newest, but I'm not the best either, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well so they don't pick me. I'd stop the gym membership and the streaming to save a bit. I wouldn't do any computer course, because I'd be useless at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot in my stomach. Not panic, just a knot that doesn't go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonas drives a van. Does this picture touch his job too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than mine, because the route planning goes to software and they'll squeeze more drops into his day. My partner Jonas already does 120 drops a day, and if software plans his route, the van company will ask for 150.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the bakery bought a new machine, would you volunteer to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd let someone younger do it. I know that's not clever. I just like what I know.

say: I'd say **offices** will feel it, not people who make things.
I'd keep my **head down** at work and post nothing.
think: I think the bakery would try to **cut a night operator** with a machine.
I think being **middling** means I could be the one picked.
do: Keep doing my **job well** so I'm not the one chosen.
Cancel the **gym** and streaming to save a bit.
Skip any **computer course**, because I'd struggle with it.
feel: A **knot** in my stomach that doesn't go away.
S1.quote: My partner Jonas already does 120 drops a day, and if software plans his route, the van company will ask for 150.
fieldNote: Fatima's household risk is double: her **night shift** and Jonas's **delivery targets**.
She admits avoiding new machines **isn't clever**, but sticks with it.
Her plan relies on being **good enough** not to be picked.

steps.text: Cancel the gym membership and streaming subscription
Keep the dough weights perfect so the bakery keeps her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and someone needs to sort it out. At work I'd say we should all stick together. I'd probably not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd lose the bakery job by 2031 and Jonas would lose the van even sooner, because the planning goes first. We'd have two incomes going at once, and nothing saved. I don't have another skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my sister Leyla if we could move in with her family for a while. I'd look for any job in a care home or a shop, anything with people. I'd apply for whatever government help is going, even though I've never claimed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened, like when you miss a step in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028, and the robots that can do your job around 2031. What happens in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office would change first: ordering flour and the shift planning would go to computers. On the floor we'd carry on until the robots arrived, and I'd spend the whole time waiting to be told. Three years of waiting for the bakery to tell me I'm finished would be worse than being told on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving, to be near more work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe to the city, but rents there are double. I'd only move if Jonas found something first.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and someone needs to sort it out.
I'd tell colleagues we should **stick together**.
think: I think I'd lose the **bakery job** by 2031, and Jonas his van sooner.
I think we'd face **two incomes** going at once with nothing saved.
do: Ask my sister **Leyla** if we can move in for a while.
Look for work in a **care home** or a shop.
Apply for **government help** for the first time.
feel: **Frightened**, like missing a step in the dark.
S2.quote: Three years of waiting for the bakery to tell me I'm finished would be worse than being told on day one.
fieldNote: The **thinking-first** order hits Jonas before her, so the household loses income early.
Fatima would find the **waiting** harder than the job loss itself.
She'd claim help for the first time, which she sees as a **big step**.

steps.text: Ask sister Leyla about moving in with her family
Apply for care home or shop jobs nearby
Claim government support for the first time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people shouldn't panic. At work I'd tell the younger ones to sort themselves out early. Me, I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be out of the bakery by 2034, just a bit later. Jonas would go first again, in 2031. It's slower, but it's the same ending for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save, maybe twenty a week, and I'd stop eating out completely. I'd wait and see what the bakery actually does, because they might not buy robots at all. Jonas could look at driving lorries, which might last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frightened. More like dread on a Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years change what you'd do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd save, because we're at zero, and I'd watch what the bakery and the van firm did. Five years only helps if my partner Jonas and I can save something first, and right now we save nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at care work. Would you train for that before you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the last year or two, when it's certain. I'd hate to do a course for nothing. My mum did care work, so I know what it is.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd tell the **younger ones** to sort themselves out early.
think: I think I'd still be **out of the bakery** by 2034.
I think it's the **same ending**, just slower, with Jonas going first.
do: Save about **twenty a week** and stop eating out.
Wait to see whether the bakery actually **buys robots**.
Look at **care work** training in the last year or two.
feel: **Dread**, like a Sunday night that never ends.
S3.quote: Five years only helps if my partner Jonas and I can save something first, and right now we save nothing.
fieldNote: The extra years don't change Fatima's expected **ending**, only the timing.
She'd **wait for certainty** before training, true to her dislike of risk.
She knows **care work** from her mother, so it's a familiar fallback.

steps.text: Save twenty a week and stop eating out
Watch whether the bakery buys robots for the night shift
Train for care work once the bakery cuts are certain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots can happen. At work I'd say let's not worry yet. I'd not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far enough that I can breathe. I'd have a few more years of steady nights and maybe Jonas and I could get a bit ahead. I'd still lose the bakery job in the end, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my nights and try to get a little cushion, maybe a month's rent. I'd think about care work when it got closer. I'd wait and see, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a cloud, but far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots around 2039. You'd be 37. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I'd want children, maybe, and that's the worry. I'd want to start a family at 37, and the bakery robots would arrive the same year the baby did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the bakery to do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us early, honestly, and pay for training. They'd save money with the robots, so they could share some of it with the people who made their bread for years.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time**, and lots can happen.
I'd tell colleagues **not to worry** yet.
think: I think I can **breathe**, with some steady years ahead.
I think I'd still **lose the bakery job** in the end.
do: Keep working **nights** and build a cushion of a month's rent.
Think about **care work** when the change gets closer.
Mostly **wait and see** what the bakery does.
feel: **Calmer**, with a cloud that's still far off.
S4.quote: I'd want to start a family at 37, and the bakery robots would arrive the same year the baby did.
fieldNote: Fatima still expects to lose the job, so her mood stays **anxious** despite feeling calmer.
The robots' arrival collides with her hope of **starting a family**.
She wants the bakery to **share savings** through notice and training.

steps.text: Save one month of rent while working nights
Wait to see the bakery's plans before choosing care work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Jonas and I would both lose work and we've got nothing saved. What would help is the bakery telling us early and paying for a course, and some help with rent while we change jobs. I'm not clever with computers, but I've made bread for seven years, and that should count for something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the night shift. People who work nights don't get to go to meetings or courses, because we're asleep when they happen. If there's training, it needs to fit us too.

headlineQuote: I'm not clever with computers, but I've made bread for seven years, and that should count for something.
portrait: Fatima, 27, runs the **dough divider** on a night shift at an industrial bakery and has less than a month saved.
Her partner Jonas drives a **delivery van**, so the household has two exposed incomes.
She avoids new tech, talks little about AI, and prefers to **wait for certainty** before acting.
She goes from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures, mainly about losing both incomes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Jonas would lose work with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Early notice** and paid training from the bakery, plus help with **rent** during a job change.
